verifiedFinding: REFINEMENT of the dispatch's premise, not a confirmation of it as stated. The engine study function, the engine-api route, AND the hauska-map BFF core (pe-flood-drainage-core.ts) already fully accept, validate, and forward rainfallDepthInches end to end -- this is NOT limited to 'the engine already answers her question.' The ONLY break in the chain is the top-level PE client function requestFloodDrainageRefresh(parcelNodeId), whose signature has no depth parameter at all, and the total absence of any UI control. Fix is scoped to hauska-map's client fn + FloodTool.tsx UI + one additive engine field (rainfallCurve) + one PDF label bug (below) -- not a new backend capability.
latentBugFound: pdf/flood-drainage.ts:1424 hardcodes the Design-storm line as `${study.rainfallDepthInches} in . 24-hr . 100-yr` regardless of actual rainfallSource. Since rainfallDepthInches is ALREADY callable with a custom parameter today via a direct API call (the engine has never rejected it), this line is ALREADY capable of printing a false '100-yr' label on any run where rainfallSource==='parameter'. Confirmed live via the empirical test below: a parameter-sourced 4in run reached this code path with rainfallSource='parameter'. Must fix as part of this row since the PDF is the surface where the false claim would leave the building.

empiricalViolationTest.method: Real direct function call to runFloodDrainageStudy (packages/engine-core/src/site-plan/flood-drainage-study.ts) with SITE_DRAINAGE_NATIVE=1 (the repo's real production fallback path for when pysheds is unavailable, not a test mock) and REAL live network fetches: fetchUsgs3depDem (live USGS 3DEP) and fetchNoaaAtlas14PointEstimate (live NOAA Atlas 14 PFDS). This is a local direct function call, not a hit against a deployed engine-api/BFF endpoint -- reported precisely per the 'local-fn-call vs live-deploy' distinction.

empiricalViolationTest.falsifier: The control would be proven INERT if rainfallDepthInches/rainfallSource in the result stayed pinned at the default (9.5in/'default') regardless of the parameter, or if no downstream stat/text changed at all.
empiricalViolationTest.verdict: NOT INERT. rainfallDepthInches, rainfallSource, the whole-region ponding stat (556064 vs 455246 sqft, -18%), the gradient note text, and the briefing sentence all changed correctly with the parameter. contradicted: the parcel-CLIPPED ponding stat (pondedAreaSqFt) was bit-identical across both runs on this specific tiny fixture parcel -- plausibly a ceiling/saturation effect on a ~0.19-acre parcel where both storm sizes already flood the full on-parcel intersection, not evidence of inertness (the wider region figure it derives from DID move); flagged as an observed-but-unexplained detail, not chased further since the D8 model itself is out of scope for this row.
empiricalViolationTest.secondMechanismConsidered: Run B's 10x speedup (183ms vs 1752ms) could look like a per-bbox DEM/study cache making a 'default' run artificially slow and a 'custom depth' run artificially fast (the dispatch's own worry). REJECTED by a third call: grep of packages/adapters/src/topography/usgs3dep.ts found zero caching code, and a third run at a DIFFERENT bbox with default depth (fresh NOAA fetch required) took 707ms, close to run A's cost profile, not close to run B's -- confirming the real driver is simply that resolveStudyRainfall SKIPS the NOAA Atlas14 network fetch entirely when a parameter is supplied (flood-drainage-study.ts:615-624), not any cache differential. A custom depth is, if anything, cheaper than default -- never the reverse.

timeoutDetermination.dispatchPremise: unverified note claiming feasibility refresh runs 85-154s while clients abort at 55s; dispatch asked whether the SAME risk applies differentially to a flood-drainage depth change specifically
timeoutDetermination.sourceOfThatNumber: 90_operations/OPS-23_surface_completion_program.md F7, doc_repo A-128 -- measured via gcloud logging on hauska-engine-api for the FEASIBILITY report's Travis-county refreshes specifically (pe-feasibility-export-handler.ts, its OWN separate FEASIBILITY_ENGINE_TIMEOUT_MS=55_000), not flood-drainage. That exact problem already has its own dedicated, separately-scoped fix in flight: P-155 / _catalog/dispatch_missions/mission_p155_feasibility_async.md (async refresh + poll routes across hauska-engine/hauska-map/legacy-design-tools), currently reopened per F23 regression -- not this row's repo set and not this row's scope.
timeoutDetermination.flooddrainageOwnBudget: pe-flood-drainage-core.ts:42 FLOOD_ENGINE_TIMEOUT_MS = 55_000 (separate constant, separate route family). No production log evidence found anywhere in doc_repo of flood-drainage's own refresh exceeding this budget -- unlike feasibility, which has 9 measured gcloud-logged requests proving the overrun.
timeoutDetermination.codeLevelAnalysis: flood-drainage-study.ts has NO refresh-level caching at any depth -- every call (default or parameter) re-fetches the DEM and re-runs the hydrology worker from scratch; the only thing 'cached' is the LAST-refreshed study JSON served instantly by the separate GET .../study read endpoint, which is orthogonal to which depth produced it. A parameter-sourced run does strictly less work than a default run (skips the NOAA round trip). There is therefore no code-level reason a depth change specifically would be more likely to time out than the default refresh already occasionally is.
timeoutDetermination.decision: Do NOT build new async-refresh/polling infrastructure for this control. Reuse the EXISTING synchronous refresh call and its EXISTING timeout/retry handling (engine_timeout/unreachable -> 503 retryable:true, FLOOD_ENGINE_TIMEOUT_RETRY_MESSAGE) for both default and parameter-sourced runs -- the control's own risk profile is no worse than the feature's existing default-depth risk profile, and that pre-existing risk is out of this row's scope (it would mean re-litigating the entire report's timeout budget, not adding a depth control). This is an evidence-based correction of the dispatch's stated premise, reported per its own instruction to 'report it rather than working around it.'
